warmup.q: A sorted set holds 128 merchants with short names, and MEMORY USAGE says it takes about 1 KB. You add one more short merchant. What happens to its memory?
options: It grows by a few bytes, the size of one more entry
It grows about tenfold, to around 11 KB
Nothing changes until the set reaches 512 members
Redis refuses the add until you raise a memory setting
warmup.why: Up to 128 members, Redis packs a sorted set into one compact block called a listpack. The 129th member crosses the default zset-max-listpack-entries (128), and Redis rebuilds the key as a hash table plus a skip list, with pointers and an allocation per member. On the lab server MEMORY USAGE went from 1,076 to 10,888 bytes. 512 is the limit for hashes and for sets of integers, not sorted sets. This lesson builds up why: in a store that lives in memory, the bookkeeping around small objects decides how much fits.

sections.h: Five core types cover most of a payment service
sections.html:
Lesson 2 ended with a server that keeps typed values in memory. This lesson asks which types a payment service needs, and how an in-memory store lays them out, because in RAM the bookkeeping around small objects decides how much fits. Start with the jobs.

A count of today's authorizations is a number you add to. Redis keeps it in a string, its basic value: any bytes up to 512 MB. When the bytes are an integer, INCR and DECRBY do the arithmetic on the server.

A payment record has fields: status, amount, currency. With only strings, you would store it as one JSON string and rewrite all of it to change the status (read, change, write back: lesson 2's race), or as one key per field and pay a round trip for each. A hash is a small map of fields inside one key. HSET payment:43 status settled changes one field on the server, and HGETALL reads them all in one round trip.

Settlement batches waiting for a worker need order: first in, first out. A list keeps insertion order and is cheap at both ends. RPUSH adds at the tail, LPOP takes from the head. (The Messaging track's lesson on Redis Streams shows why Streams make a better queue.)

The cards the fraud team flagged today need membership: is this card in the group or not? A set holds unique members. SADD adds, SISMEMBER checks, and adding a member twice changes nothing.

Merchants ranked by approvals need order by a number that keeps changing. A sorted set holds unique members, each with a number called its score, and keeps them sorted by score. ZINCRBY bumps a score, ZRANGE reads the top ten.

Cost matters as much as shape, because every command runs on lesson 2's single thread. Redis writes costs in Big-O notation, where N is the number of elements in the key. O(1) means the work doesn't grow with the key. O(N) means it grows in step with it: twice the elements, twice the work. O(log N) grows very slowly: doubling N adds one step. M is the number of elements a command returns.

Type Example key Main commands Cost
string card:7:status, auths:today GET, SET, INCR O(1)
hash payment:43 HGET, HSET, HINCRBY O(1) per field, HGETALL O(N)
list settlement:queue RPUSH, LPOP, LRANGE O(1) at either end
set fraud:flagged SADD, SISMEMBER, SINTER O(1) add and check, SMEMBERS O(N)
sorted set merchants:approved ZADD, ZINCRBY, ZRANGE O(log N), ranges O(log N + M)

Key names are plain strings. The habit is type:id with colons, such as payment:43 or merchant:m-17:approved. Redis doesn't care, but a shared prefix lets SCAN MATCH payment:* find a family of keys, and your teammates can read it.

try.title: Use each type once
steps: Start the server if it isn't running (docker compose -f env/redis.yml up -d from the labs folder) and open docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli.
Type the commands below. Before each one, say what it will print.
Predict the last one: what happens when you GET a hash?

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
SET card:7:status active
HSET payment:43 status approved amount 1250 currency EUR
RPUSH settlement:queue batch-1 batch-2 batch-3
LPOP settlement:queue
SADD fraud:flagged card:7 card:9 card:7
SCARD fraud:flagged
SISMEMBER fraud:flagged card:9
ZADD merchants:approved 42 m-17 40 m-03 12 m-88
ZRANGE merchants:approved 0 -1 REV WITHSCORES
TYPE settlement:queue
GET payment:43

try.expect: RPUSH returns the new length, (integer) 3, and LPOP hands back "batch-1", the oldest entry. SADD returns (integer) 2: the second card:7 was already there, so SCARD says 2. SISMEMBER returns (integer) 1 (true). ZRANGE ... REV WITHSCORES lists m-17 42, m-03 40, m-88 12, highest first. TYPE settlement:queue says list. GET payment:43 fails with (error) WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value: GET is a string command, and the key holds a hash.

sections.h: Small keys live in a listpack, big ones in a hash table or skip list
sections.html:
Picture a hash with three fields stored the way java.util.HashMap stores entries: a table of slots, one entry object per field, and separately allocated strings for each field and value, all joined by 8-byte pointers. Every allocation also carries a header. For status approved amount 1250 currency EUR, 35 bytes of actual data, the bookkeeping outweighs the data. Multiply by ten million payment records and much of your RAM holds pointers.

The simplest fix is to drop the structure: write the entries one after another into a single block of memory, each with its length in front, and find a field by reading from the start. That is a listpack. On the lab server the three-field hash took 77 bytes as a listpack and 215 bytes as a hash table. The price is the search: finding a field means walking the block, which is O(N). For a hundred short entries in about a kilobyte of contiguous memory, the walk is cheap, because the CPU reads contiguous bytes fast.

Where does it break? At size. Walking 10,000 entries on every HGET, on the one thread every client shares, is too slow, and inserting into the middle of a big block means moving every byte after it. So Redis uses both layouts: a listpack while the key is small, the general structure once it grows. TYPE still says hash. What changes is the encoding, the layout behind the type, which OBJECT ENCODING reports.

For a big hash or set, the general structure is a hash table. A big sorted set needs two things at once: find a member's score fast, and keep members in score order. A sorted array would give fast lookups by position, but inserting would shift everything after the new member. A linked list inserts cheaply, but finding the place means walking it. Redis keeps two structures holding the same members: a hash table from member to score, and a skip list, a linked list in score order where some nodes carry extra links that jump far ahead, like express lanes. A search rides the top lane and drops down a lane when it would overshoot, so finding a position takes O(log N). Sets of plain integers have their own compact form, the intset, a sorted array searched by binary search. Big lists become a quicklist: a linked list of listpacks of up to 8 KB each.

These are the 8.10 defaults:

Setting Default Becomes
hash-max-listpack-entries and -value 512 fields, 64 bytes hashtable
set-max-intset-entries 512 integers hashtable
set-max-listpack-entries and -value 128 members, 64 bytes hashtable
zset-max-listpack-entries and -value 128 members, 64 bytes skiplist
list-max-listpack-size -2, meaning 8 KB quicklist

Either limit triggers the switch: too many entries, or one entry longer than the value limit. A single 65-byte member turns a two-member sorted set into a skip list. The switch goes one way only: remove members until the key is tiny again, and it keeps the big encoding. And it costs memory. On the lab server a sorted set of 128 short members took 1,076 bytes, and the 129th member made it 10,888.

Strings have encodings too: int for a number that fits in 64 bits, embstr for a short string kept in one allocation with its header, and raw for longer ones.

frames.say: Three merchants, one key. Redis stores the small sorted set as a listpack: one block of memory, the entries packed back to back in score order, each carrying its own length. No pointers, no per-entry allocations. MEMORY USAGE says 68 bytes.

The skip list keeps members in score order, and some nodes carry express links that jump ahead. A search starts in the top lane, moves right while the next score is smaller, and drops a lane when it would overshoot: O(log N). Each link also stores how many nodes it skips, so the rank comes out of the same walk. The price: 10,813 bytes, eight times more than at 128 members.

try.title: Watch a sorted set change shape
steps: At the redis-cli prompt, run the commands below one at a time. The first four ask how keys from the previous Try it are stored. The EVAL adds 128 members in one go.
Before ZADD board 129 m-129, predict the encoding and the memory after it.
Before the last OBJECT ENCODING small, predict what one 65-character member does to a two-member set. (Paste 65 x's or any 65-character string.)

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
SET auths:today 41
OBJECT ENCODING auths:today
OBJECT ENCODING card:7:status
OBJECT ENCODING payment:43
EVAL "for i = 1, 128 do redis.call('ZADD', KEYS[1], i, 'm-' .. i) end" 1 board
OBJECT ENCODING board
MEMORY USAGE board
ZADD board 129 m-129
OBJECT ENCODING board
MEMORY USAGE board
ZREM board m-129
OBJECT ENCODING board
ZADD small 1 m-1
OBJECT ENCODING small
ZADD small 2 xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
OBJECT ENCODING small
CONFIG GET zset-max-listpack-*

try.expect: auths:today is "int" (the value is a number, so Redis stores it as one), card:7:status is "embstr", and the three-field payment:43 is "listpack". With 128 members, board is "listpack" at (integer) 1076 bytes. After the 129th it is "skiplist" at (integer) 10888, about ten times more. After ZREM it is back to 128 members and still "skiplist". small starts as "listpack" and becomes "skiplist" with only two members, because one member is longer than 64 bytes. CONFIG GET shows the two limits: zset-max-listpack-entries 128 and zset-max-listpack-value 64. Byte counts can differ by a few percent between Redis builds.

video.title: Listpacks, hash tables and skip lists

sections.h: Every key also costs a slot in the keyspace's hash table
sections.html:
Encodings shrink what is inside a key. Every key also has a fixed cost, because the whole keyspace is one big hash table from key name to value. In-memory caches mostly hold small objects. In Twitter's study of 153 cache clusters, the median cluster's average key was under 38 bytes and its average value about 230 bytes, and Memcached spends 56 bytes of bookkeeping on every item. At those sizes the fixed cost per key decides how many keys fit in RAM.

Here Redis and Valkey have parted ways. Redis 7.2, the version Valkey forked from, keeps the keyspace in a chained hash table: an array of buckets, each pointing to a separately allocated entry, which points to the key and to the value. A lookup follows about four pointers, and each one can be a trip to RAM, lesson 1's 100 ns rung. Valkey 8.1 replaced it with buckets of 64 bytes, one CPU cache line each. A bucket holds up to seven entries plus one byte of each entry's hash, which rules out almost every wrong candidate without following its pointer, and the key is stored inside the value's own object. A lookup touches about two memory locations instead of four. Redis 8 cut its own per-key cost by a different route. On the lab machine, 100,000 tiny keys cost 75 bytes each on Redis 7.2.4, 55 on Redis 8.10.3 and 46 on Valkey 9.1.3, and a TTL added 20 to 35 bytes more.

The table also has to grow. Doubling a table of 10 million buckets in one go would hold the only thread for a long time, so both servers rehash incrementally. They keep the old and the new table side by side. Every command that touches the table moves a few buckets across, a short timed step on the server's background timer moves more, and lookups check both tables until the old one is empty. Redis also avoids resizing while a forked child is writing a snapshot, because moving memory then makes the kernel copy pages (lesson 9). Valkey's developers kept incremental rehashing, SCAN's cursor and the random sampling of keys that eviction depends on (lesson 5), and those needs are why they wrote their own table instead of taking an off-the-shelf one.

try.title: Weigh a key on Redis 8.10 and on Valkey 9.1
steps: Run the script below in a terminal. It starts a throwaway Redis 8.10.3 and a throwaway Valkey 9.1.3 (the first run downloads the Valkey image), writes 100,000 tiny keys into each, without and then with a TTL, prints the memory per key from used_memory, and removes both containers.
Before it prints, predict which server stores a key in fewer bytes, and how much a TTL adds.
Notice that one script talks to both servers: the Valkey image also ships redis-cli as an alias for valkey-cli.

code.title: terminal
code.html: # one throwaway server of each, then 100,000 tiny keys in each, with and without a TTL docker run --rm -d --name sfz-redis-mem -m 256m redis:8.10.3 > /dev/null docker run --rm -d --name sfz-valkey-mem -m 256m valkey/valkey:9.1.3 > /dev/null sleep 2 used() { docker exec "$1" redis-cli INFO memory | grep '^used_memory:' | tr -dc '0-9'; } for c in sfz-redis-mem sfz-valkey-mem; do for args in "" ", 'EX', 3600"; do docker exec "$c" redis-cli FLUSHALL > /dev/null before=$(used "$c") docker exec "$c" redis-cli EVAL "for i = 1, 100000 do redis.call('SET', 'idem:' .. i, 'done'$args) end return 1" 0 > /dev/null echo "$c${args:+ with TTL}: $(( ($(used "$c") - before) / 100000 )) bytes per key" done done docker rm -f sfz-redis-mem sfz-valkey-mem > /dev/null

try.expect: On the lab machine: sfz-redis-mem: 55 bytes per key, sfz-redis-mem with TTL: 79 bytes per key (84 in a second run, depending on where the deadline table was in its growth), sfz-valkey-mem: 46 bytes per key and sfz-valkey-mem with TTL: 66 bytes per key. Each key name is about 10 bytes and each value the 4-byte string done, so most of what you pay for is bookkeeping. The same script against redis:7.2.4, the version Valkey forked from, printed 75 and 108: both servers have cut the per-key cost since they split, and Valkey a little further.

Yang et al., A large scale analysis of hundreds of in-memory cache clusters at Twitter (OSDI 2020)

sections.h: A sorted set orders by score, then by member
sections.html:
Rank 20,000 merchants by approved payments, refreshed every second on a dashboard. In SQL you would run ORDER BY approvals DESC LIMIT 10 each time, and the database would sort or walk an index on every refresh. A sorted set does the ordering on write instead: every ZINCRBY moves the member to its new place, so reading the top ten is reading the first ten entries.

ZINCRBY merchants:approved 1 m-17 adds one approval to merchant m-17, creating the member if it is new. ZRANGE merchants:approved 0 9 REV WITHSCORES returns the top ten with their scores, highest first (REV reverses the default low-to-high order). ZREVRANK merchants:approved m-17 returns its place counted from the top.

Three details cause most leaderboard bugs.

Ranks start at 0. ZREVRANK returns 0 for the leader, so add one before a person sees it.

Ties are ordered by member, byte by byte. In ascending order, m-anna comes before m-bert when both have 5. REV flips the whole order, ties included, so m-bert comes first. If the product wants "whoever got there first wins the tie", the member name can't give you that; you have to fold time into the score (see Go deeper).

Scores are doubles, 64-bit floating-point numbers. Whole numbers are exact up to 2^53, about 9 × 10^15, which is plenty for counts and for amounts in cents. Fractions are not exact, so store cents, never euros with decimals.

Since Redis 6.2, ZRANGE takes REV, BYSCORE, BYLEX and LIMIT, and the docs mark ZREVRANGE and ZRANGEBYSCORE as deprecated. Since 7.2, ZRANK and ZREVRANK accept WITHSCORE and return rank and score in one round trip. Under the hood, from the encodings above: ZSCORE asks the hash table, O(1); ZADD, ZREVRANK and ZRANGE walk the skip list, O(log N), plus M for the members a range returns. In Jedis:

Java
List<Tuple> top = redis.zrangeWithScores("merchants:approved", ZRangeParams.zrangeParams(0, 9).rev());
KeyValue<Long, Double> me = redis.zrevrankWithScore("merchants:approved", "m-17");   // null if absent
Kotlin
val top: List<Tuple> = redis.zrangeWithScores("merchants:approved", ZRangeParams.zrangeParams(0, 9).rev())
val me: KeyValue<Long, Double>? = redis.zrevrankWithScore("merchants:approved", "m-17")   // null if absent

try.title: Rank four merchants, two of them tied
steps: Add four merchants. m-anna and m-bert both have 5.
Predict the order of the two ZRANGE calls before you run them, ties included.
Run the rest. What rank does m-anna have, and does it count from 0 or 1?

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
ZADD merchants:today 5 m-anna 5 m-bert 7 m-cora 3 m-dave
ZRANGE merchants:today 0 -1 WITHSCORES
ZRANGE merchants:today 0 -1 REV WITHSCORES
ZREVRANK merchants:today m-anna WITHSCORE
ZINCRBY merchants:today 1 m-anna
ZRANGE merchants:today 0 2 REV WITHSCORES
ZREVRANK merchants:today m-zed

try.expect: Ascending, the order is m-dave 3, m-anna 5, m-bert 5, m-cora 7: the tie goes to the smaller member name. With REV it is m-cora, m-bert, m-anna, m-dave: the tie flips too. ZREVRANK ... WITHSCORE returns 1) (integer) 2 and 2) "5", so m-anna is third, counted from 0. After ZINCRBY it has "6" and the top three are m-cora 7, m-anna 6, m-bert 5. A member that doesn't exist gets (nil).

sections.h: Big keys turn O(N) commands into outages
sections.html:
Put lesson 2's model next to this lesson's Big-O table and you get the most common Redis outage. An O(N) command on a key with a big N holds the only thread for as long as it runs. Nobody writes a slow SMEMBERS on purpose. A set of flagged cards starts with 50 members, grows for two years, and one day holds a million. The code that reads it in one call never changed.

On the lab server a set of a million card ids took about 30 MB. Reading it whole with SMEMBERS held the event loop for about 54 ms, and freeing it with DEL took about 40 ms. For those milliseconds every other client of that Redis waited. Run the same read from a few pods at once and the waits add up.

Four habits keep you out of trouble:

  • Read big collections in pages with a cursor: SSCAN, HSCAN, ZSCAN, and SCAN for the whole keyspace. Each call returns a small batch plus a cursor to continue from, so each does a bounded amount of work and other clients get their turn in between. For sorted sets, ZRANGE with small ranges does the same.
  • Delete big keys with UNLINK. It removes the key from the keyspace at once and frees the memory on the bio_lazy_free background thread.
  • Split by something natural: one set per day, one hash per merchant, one sorted set per region. Ten keys of 100,000 members are kinder to everyone than one key of a million.
  • Find big keys before they find you, with MEMORY USAGE key and redis-cli --bigkeys, which walks the keyspace with SCAN.

The encoding limits give you a second reason to keep keys small: below them, the same data takes a fraction of the memory.

try.title: Build a big key and time it
steps: At the redis-cli prompt, run the first three commands. The EVAL builds a set of a million card ids. It takes most of a second, and blocks the server the whole time.
In a second terminal, read the whole set once and throw the output away: docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli SMEMBERS flagged:cards > /dev/null.
Back at the prompt, run the rest: build a copy, delete one set with DEL and the other with UNLINK, then read the slow log. Predict which commands it lists.
Clean up afterwards with FLUSHALL if you like. This is your own lab server.

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
SLOWLOG RESET
EVAL "for i = 1, 1000000 do redis.call('SADD', KEYS[1], 'card:' .. i) end return redis.call('SCARD', KEYS[1])" 1 flagged:cards
MEMORY USAGE flagged:cards
EVAL "for i = 1, 1000000 do redis.call('SADD', KEYS[1], 'card:' .. i) end return 1" 1 flagged:copy
DEL flagged:cards
UNLINK flagged:copy
SLOWLOG GET 5

try.expect: The slow log lists commands that ran longer than 10 ms. Each entry starts with an id, a Unix timestamp, the duration in microseconds and the command. On the lab server: both EVALs about 640,000 µs, SMEMBERS about 54,000 µs, DEL about 40,000 µs. UNLINK is missing, because it returned in well under 10 ms and left the freeing to the background thread. Your numbers depend on your CPU. MEMORY USAGE printed about 37 MB: it samples a few members and extrapolates, so treat it as a rough size.

refs.title: Diagnosing latency issues (big keys and slow commands)

analogy: Encodings are a shop owner's stock book. With twenty products, one page is enough: the owner runs a finger down it, and it costs one sheet of paper. At two thousand products the page is hopeless, so the owner switches to a box of index cards sorted by name plus a ranked list on the wall. That takes far more paper, but any lookup is quick. Redis makes the same switch for you, at a size you can configure. The analogy breaks in two places: Redis switches at an exact count, and it never switches back, even after the shop shrinks.
world: The five types map onto jobs your payment services already have. Idempotency keys and per-card counters are strings. A cached card-issuer response or a payment record is a hash. Settlement batches waiting for a worker could sit in a list. The cards the fraud team flagged today are a set, and SISMEMBER checks one in O(1) on every authorization. Merchant rankings and "BINs (card number prefixes) with the most declines this hour" are sorted sets. The encoding limits matter when you size an instance: a million payment hashes of 12 fields each stay listpacks and take a fraction of the memory that a million 600-field hashes would. And look out for keys that grow without bound, like one set of every card ever flagged. That is the key that turns into a 50 ms SMEMBERS two years from now.
mistake: The most common mistake is keeping everything in one big key because it is convenient: all flagged cards in one set, all sessions in one hash, every event in one list. It works in test, where the key holds a hundred members, and fails in production, where it holds millions and an innocent HGETALL, SMEMBERS or DEL blocks the server for tens of milliseconds. It happens because Redis types feel like in-memory collections, and reading a whole HashMap in the JVM is cheap. In Redis that read holds the only command thread. Bound every key: split by day, merchant or region, read with the SCAN family, and delete big keys with UNLINK.

compare.title: The leaderboard's top N in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Leaderboard.java
java.html: public record Standing(String merchant, long approvals, long rank) {} public List<Standing> top(int n) { List<Tuple> rows = redis.zrangeWithScores(key, ZRangeParams.zrangeParams(0, n - 1).rev()); List<Standing> out = new ArrayList<>(rows.size()); for (int i = 0; i < rows.size(); i++) { Tuple t = rows.get(i); out.add(new Standing(t.getElement(), (long) t.getScore(), i + 1)); // ranks start at 1 for people } return out; }

kotlin.title: Leaderboard.kt
kotlin.html: data class Standing(val merchant: String, val approvals: Long, val rank: Long) fun top(n: Int): List<Standing> = redis.zrangeWithScores(key, ZRangeParams.zrangeParams(0, n - 1).rev()) .mapIndexed { i, t -> Standing(t.element, t.score.toLong(), i + 1L) } // ranks start at 1 for people

compare.note: The Redis call is the same in both: one ZRANGE ... REV WITHSCORES. Kotlin reads Jedis's getters as properties (t.element, t.score), and a data class replaces the record. Watch nullability at the boundary. zrevrank returns a Java Long that is null when the member doesn't exist, and Kotlin sees it as a platform type. Declare it Long? so the compiler makes you handle the null. Pass it unchecked to something that wants a Long, and you get a NullPointerException the first time a merchant has no entry.

worked.title: Keep a per-merchant sorted set small on purpose

steps.say: The fraud team wants, for each merchant, the card BINs (the first six digits of a card number) with the most declines this hour. A sorted set per merchant and hour fits: the member is the BIN, the score counts declines. About 20,000 merchants are active in an hour, and a busy one sees declines from 300 different BINs.
steps.code: String key = "declines:" + merchant + ":h" + hour; // declines:m-17:h14 redis.zincrby(key, 1, bin);

alt.html: val key = "declines:$merchant:h$hour" // declines:m-17:h14 redis.zincrby(key, 1.0, bin)

steps.say: Size it before you ship it. 300 members is past zset-max-listpack-entries, so a busy merchant's key is a skip list. On the lab server a 300-BIN set took 25,223 bytes, and a 100-BIN set took 730 bytes as a listpack (short numeric members pack tightly). Across 20,000 merchants that is about 500 MB against about 15 MB.

The dashboard shows the top 20. So keep the 100 highest and drop the rest after every increment. The key never passes 101 members and stays a listpack. A BIN that falls off and comes back starts again from 1, which is fine for a "most declines" view. Trimming a key that is already a skip list would not help: it stays a skip list.
steps.code: redis.zincrby(key, 1, bin); redis.zremrangeByRank(key, 0, -101); // keep the 100 highest; the key never passes 101 members

alt.html: redis.zincrby(key, 1.0, bin) redis.zremrangeByRank(key, 0, -101) // keep the 100 highest; the key never passes 101 members

steps.say: Read the top 20 with one ZRANGE, and give the key a lifetime so old hours clean themselves up (lesson 5 covers expiry). These are two separate commands per decline, so another client can run between them. Here that only means the trim runs a moment late. The Transactions track's lesson on serial execution shows how to make increment-and-trim one atomic step with a script.
steps.code: List<Tuple> top20 = redis.zrangeWithScores(key, ZRangeParams.zrangeParams(0, 19).rev()); redis.expire(key, 7_200); // two hours, then Redis deletes the key

alt.html: val top20 = redis.zrangeWithScores(key, ZRangeParams.zrangeParams(0, 19).rev()) redis.expire(key, 7_200) // two hours, then Redis deletes the key

lab.title: Catch the encoding switch, then build a merchant leaderboard
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. All 14 fail. They run against the shared Redis 8.10 container, and each test gets its own key prefix.
In EncodingProbe.java, write describe with objectEncoding and memoryUsage.

Write growUntilConverted: add element 1 and describe the key, then loop from 2 to maxSize: add, describe, and return a Transition as soon as the encoding changes. Run EncodingProbeTest. Its tests pin the 8.10 defaults: 129 for sorted sets and sets of strings, 513 for hashes and sets of integers, and one long member converting at once.
In Leaderboard.kt, write record with zincrby and top with one zrangeWithScores call using ZRangeParams.zrangeParams(0, n - 1).rev(). Turn 0-based positions into ranks that start at 1.
Write standingOf with zrevrankWithScore, and around with zrevrank and one range around that rank. Run all the tests.
hints: OBJECT ENCODING comes back as a lowercase String. Compare encodings with equals, not ==.
zrevrankWithScore returns a KeyValue<Long, Double>: key is the 0-based rank and value the score. It is null when the merchant has no entry.
In around, the range starts at max(0, rank - radius). You don't need to clamp the end: ZRANGE stops at the last member.
Scores are doubles. toLong() is safe here, because the totals are whole numbers far below 2^53.

drill.title: Top five and a rank, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the Jedis calls for two questions about merchants:approved: print the top 5 merchants with their totals, highest first, numbered from 1; and get the 1-based rank of m-17, or null if it has no entry. Then compare. Did you remember that ranks start at 0?

answer.html: List<Tuple> top5 = redis.zrangeWithScores("merchants:approved", ZRangeParams.zrangeParams(0, 4).rev()); for (int i = 0; i < top5.size(); i++) { System.out.printf("%d. %s %d%n", i + 1, top5.get(i).getElement(), (long) top5.get(i).getScore()); } Long rank = redis.zrevrank("merchants:approved", "m-17"); // 0-based, null if absent Long shown = rank == null ? null : rank + 1;

alt.html: val top5 = redis.zrangeWithScores("merchants:approved", ZRangeParams.zrangeParams(0, 4).rev()) top5.forEachIndexed { i, t -> println("${i + 1}. ${t.element} ${t.score.toLong()}") } val rank: Long? = redis.zrevrank("merchants:approved", "m-17") // 0-based, null if absent val shown = rank?.plus(1)

recap: Five types cover most jobs: strings, hashes, lists, sets and sorted sets. Choose by the operation you need, then check its cost.

Small hashes, sets and sorted sets are listpacks, and small sets of integers are intsets. Past 128 or 512 entries, or one value over 64 bytes, Redis converts them to hash tables or skip lists, and never converts back.

The keyspace is one big hash table, so every key carries fixed bookkeeping: about 75 bytes per tiny key on Redis 7.2.4, 55 on Redis 8.10 and 46 on Valkey 9.1, whose 8.1 release moved to cache-line-sized buckets.
The conversion costs memory: on the lab server a 128-member sorted set took about 1 KB, and the 129-member one about 11 KB.
Sorted sets order by score, then by member bytes, and REV flips both. Ranks start at 0. Scores are doubles, exact for whole numbers up to 2^53.
Big keys make O(N) commands block everyone. Page with the SCAN family, delete with UNLINK, and split keys by day, merchant or region.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why MEMORY USAGE of their sorted set jumped from about 1 KB to about 11 KB when it went from 128 to 129 members, and whether deleting members will bring it back down. Explain.
explain.answer: Up to 128 members (the default zset-max-listpack-entries), Redis stores a sorted set as a listpack: one block of memory with the entries packed back to back, no pointers, searched from the start. That is cheap for a small set. The 129th member makes Redis convert the key to the general form: a hash table from member to score plus a skip list in score order. Every member now has its own nodes, pointers and hash table slot, so the same data takes about ten times the memory. In exchange, lookups and ranks become O(1) and O(log N) instead of a scan. Deleting members won't bring it back: Redis only converts upward. If we want the compact form, we have to keep the key under 128 members from the start, for example by trimming after each insert, or rebuild it into a new key.

deeper.html:
Two pieces of folklore are out of date. Old posts put the embstr cut-off at 44 bytes. In Redis 8.10 a 44-byte value under a 1-character key came out raw, and so did a 35-byte value under a 41-character key, because the cut-off now depends on the key's length as well. Old posts also say ziplist: Redis 7.0 replaced ziplist with listpack, and the old *-ziplist-* setting names still work as aliases.

To break ties by time, fold time into the score. Say the product wants the merchant that reached a total first to rank higher. Use score = approvals × 100,000 + (99,999 − second of the day). A day has 86,400 seconds, so the time part fits in five digits, and a higher total always wins. Between equal totals, the earlier second gives the bigger score. Doubles stay exact up to 2^53, so totals up to about 90 billion are safe. The catch: every new approval must rewrite the time part too, which is read, compute and write. Two clients can interleave that, so do it in a Lua script (the Transactions track's lesson on serial execution) or accept small errors.

The value limits count bytes, not characters. In UTF-8 an accented letter such as é takes two bytes, so a 40-character merchant name full of them can cross the 64-byte zset-max-listpack-value.

Raising the limits is allowed. CONFIG SET zset-max-listpack-entries 256 keeps bigger sets compact, at the cost of O(N) inserts and lookups on longer blocks. The defaults are a sensible trade, and you should measure before you change them. Existing keys are not converted when you change the setting; it applies the next time a key would grow.

Redis keeps squeezing the big encodings too. The 8.6 release notes list a substantial memory reduction for hashtable-encoded hashes and skiplist-encoded sorted sets. Redis 8.10 added a new hash encoding for many hashes that share the same field names, loaded with HIMPORT. Plain HSET keys, like the ones in this lesson's lab, still show listpack and hashtable.

Valkey's write-up of its new table explains why it didn't adopt a ready-made design such as a Swiss table. The keyspace has to support incremental rehashing, a SCAN cursor that survives a resize, and picking random keys for eviction and for the expiry cycle, and off-the-shelf tables offer none of that. The developers report that speed changed very little either way: the win was memory, roughly 20 bytes per key and 30 per key with a TTL against the old layout, plus 10 to 20 bytes per element inside big hashes, sets and sorted sets.
